analysis.one_liner: Orders a federal study of hidden price-linked fees across the prescription drug supply chain.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced January 29, 2026 by Sen. Michael Bennet with one Republican cosponsor and was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directs the Government Accountability Office, the investigative arm of Congress, to study how compensation in the prescription drug supply chain is tied to a drug's price. That includes pharmacy benefit managers, insurers, wholesalers, pharmacies, manufacturers, and consultants, and it specifically looks at whether fees charged as a percentage of a drug's price reward picking and distributing more expensive drugs. The results, with recommendations for legislation, would be due to Congress two years after enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and taxpayers, if the study's findings lead to legislation that curbs price-linked fees in the drug supply chain. Percentage-of-price fees give every intermediary in the chain a reason to prefer costlier drugs, a cost that flows into premiums and out-of-pocket payments.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Comptroller General to study the type, magnitude, and prevalence of compensation and payment structures tied to a drug's price across every intermediary in the prescription drug supply chain.
Directs the study to examine conflicts of interest, including whether fees set as a percentage of a drug's price advantage the selection, distribution, or purchasing of higher-priced drugs.

Requires the study to cover affiliated versus unaffiliated entities, business models for each intermediary category, price-based compensation in both Medicare Part D and Medicaid, and trends over time.
Requires a report to Congress within two years of enactment with recommendations for legislation and administrative action.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and other intermediaries whose percentage-of-price fees would face scrutiny, if the study's recommendations became law. The study itself imposes no immediate cost beyond GAO staff time.

drawbacks.text: The bill changes no policy on its own; it only commissions a study, with findings due two years after enactment and no requirement that Congress act on the recommendations.

A report that takes two years gives intermediaries like pharmacy benefit managers a long runway under current fee structures, and past GAO reports on the drug supply chain have not by themselves produced reform.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a low-cost first step rather than a fix. Its value depends entirely on whether the Finance Committee and Congress later act on the GAO's recommendations, and the two-year timeline delays any relief for patients paying prices inflated by price-linked fees. It is worth supporting as groundwork, but it should not be confused with regulation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Michael Bennet introduced the bill on January 29, 2026, for himself and Sen. James Lankford.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day, and no further action appears in the record.
One Republican senator, Lankford of Oklahoma, cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained or lost yet. Intermediaries in the drug supply chain benefit from the delay, since the percentage-of-price fee structures the bill targets remain untouched while the bill sits in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug supply chain intermediaries, so far

for.name: Sen. Michael Bennet
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing a GAO study of price-related compensation in the prescription drug supply chain.

for.name: Sen. James Lankford
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has one Democrat and one Republican sponsor, so there is no partisan split on record; it simply has not moved since referral.

industries.note: The study directly targets the compensation structures of PBMs, including fees calculated as a percentage of a drug's price, which grow when drugs are more expensive. If the findings lead to legislation, PBMs could lose a revenue model that rewards higher drug prices.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D insurers and plan sponsors
industries.note: Plan sponsors pay and receive price-linked compensation that the study would map, including contracts with PBMs and the consultants who audit them. Insurers could benefit if reform lowers their drug costs, but they are also part of the fee chain under examination.

industries.industry: Drug wholesalers, pharmacies, manufacturers, and rebate aggregators
industries.note: The study would document each category's business model and compensation tied to drug prices. Manufacturers benefit today from intermediaries that favor high-priced drugs, while pharmacies and wholesalers would see their payment structures put under a public microscope.

industries.industry: Benefit consultants, brokers, auditors, and pharmacy services administrative organizations
industries.note: The bill names these advisors explicitly for study, including whether their fees tied to drug prices create conflicts of interest. Price-based compensation is a revenue stream for them, so scrutiny threatens it.

analysis.trajectory: With no action since its January 2026 referral and no committee schedule on record, the bill will most likely sit in the Finance Committee unless the chair takes it up; study bills of this kind rarely reach the floor without a committee push, and the two-year reporting clock would not even begin until enactment.
